content: When the baby was born, toward whom did the women of the town direct their praise?
options: The LORD
Boaz
Ruth
The nearest kinsman-redeemer
explanation: Ruth 4:14 records the women saying to Naomi: 'Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer.' The praise was directed to the LORD. 'Boaz' was the husband but is not the object of praise in this verse (wrong_detail). 'Ruth' is praised in the following verse, not in this one (near_passage). 'The nearest kinsman-redeemer' in this verse refers to the baby himself, not to the one being honored (wrong_detail).

content: What did Naomi do with the baby after he was born?
options: She took him in her arms and became his nurse
She brought him to the nearest kinsman-redeemer
She handed him over to the women of the town
She named him Boaz
explanation: Ruth 4:16 states: 'Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse.' The answer 'brought him to the nearest kinsman-redeemer' is wrong because the nearest kinsman had already refused his right of redemption earlier in the chapter (wrong_scope). 'Handed him over to the women of the town' contradicts the text, since Naomi herself nursed the child (wrong_detail). 'Named him Boaz' is wrong on both the person who named him and the name itself, since the neighboring women named him Obed (wrong_detail).

content: Who gave Ruth's baby his name?
options: The neighboring women
Boaz
Naomi
The elders at the gate
explanation: Ruth 4:17 states: 'And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying... they named him Obed.' So it was the neighboring women who gave the name. 'Boaz' was the father but is not identified as the one who named the child in the text (wrong_detail). 'Naomi' held and nursed the baby but did not name him (near_passage). 'The elders at the gate' belonged to the earlier land-redemption transaction and have no connection to the naming of the child (wrong_scope).

content: The women said that Ruth was more valuable to Naomi than what?
options: Seven sons
All the wealth in the land
The nearest kinsman-redeemer
All other daughters-in-law
explanation: Ruth 4:15 declares that Ruth is 'more to you than seven sons' to Naomi, because she loved her and bore the child who restored life to her. The number seven signifies completeness in Hebrew idiom, making this the highest possible praise. 'All the wealth in the land' sounds plausible but does not appear anywhere in the text (common_misconception). 'The nearest kinsman-redeemer' confuses this verse with the redemption theme from the earlier passage (near_passage). 'All other daughters-in-law' misidentifies the comparison, since the text compares Ruth to seven sons, not to other daughters-in-law (wrong_detail).

content: According to the women, what would the newborn child bring to Naomi in her old age?
options: Restore her life and nourish her
A dowry so she could remarry
Inheritance rights to land in Moab
Protection from the kinsman-redeemer
explanation: Ruth 4:15 states that the child 'will restore your life and nourish your old age.' The child is the source of comfort and sustenance for Naomi. 'A dowry so she could remarry' is entirely wrong because Naomi does not remarry (common_misconception). 'Inheritance rights to land in Moab' confuses the location, since the redeemed inheritance was in Bethlehem, not Moab (wrong_detail). 'Protection from the kinsman-redeemer' misunderstands the role, since the nearer kinsman had already withdrawn and was no longer a threat (wrong_scope).

content: When naming the child, what did the women declare about his relationship to Naomi?
options: A son has been born to Naomi
The child would belong to Boaz's lineage
The child must be returned to Ruth
Naomi would give him to the redeemer
explanation: Ruth 4:17 states: 'A son has been born to Naomi,' showing that the child Obed was counted as Naomi's son to carry on the lineage of her deceased husband and sons. 'Belonging to Boaz's lineage' is true regarding bloodline but is not what the women declared in this verse (true_but_off). 'Must be returned to Ruth' contradicts the fact that Naomi was nursing him (wrong_detail). 'Naomi would give him to the redeemer' wrongly links to the theme of redeeming property from the earlier passage (near_passage).

content: What reason did the women give to explain why Ruth was so precious to Naomi?
options: Because she loved Naomi and had borne the child
Because she was wealthier than Boaz
Because she was a pure-blooded Israelite
Because she had redeemed the property
explanation: Ruth 4:15 gives the reason: her daughter-in-law 'loves you' and has borne the child herself, making her more precious than seven sons. 'Wealthier than Boaz' is wrong because Ruth was a poor woman who had been gleaning in the fields (wrong_detail). 'A pure-blooded Israelite' directly contradicts the text, since she was a Moabite woman (common_misconception). 'Had redeemed the property' wrongly assigns Boaz's role to Ruth (near_passage).

content: In Ruth 4:13-17, where is the LORD's role in the story most clearly emphasized?
options: He caused Ruth to conceive and was praised by the people
He appeared and spoke directly to Naomi
He issued a command requiring Boaz to marry Ruth
He sent an angel to name the newborn child
explanation: Comparing the verses: 4:13 records 'the LORD gave her conception,' and 4:14 the women exclaim 'Blessed be the LORD.' Thus the LORD's role is expressed through granting conception and being praised by the people, not through dramatic intervention. 'Appeared and spoke directly to Naomi' is almost plausible but is nowhere found in this passage (wrong_detail). 'Issued a command requiring Boaz to marry Ruth' is also almost plausible, since Boaz acted voluntarily as redeemer according to the law, not under a direct divine command (common_misconception). 'Sent an angel to name the child' is wrong because it was the neighboring women who named the child Obed (wrong_detail).

content: Analyzing the women's blessing in 4:14-15, which concern of Naomi from the beginning of the book is resolved through the birth of the child?
options: The emptiness of losing her husband and sons with no one left to continue the lineage
Her having been driven out of the land of Moab years before
Her fear that Boaz would eventually abandon Ruth
The land debt she still owed to the elders
explanation: Naomi had lamented that she went away 'full' but returned 'empty,' having lost her husband and two sons; the blessing of 4:14-15 declares she 'shall not be without a redeemer' and the child 'will restore your life and nourish your old age,' resolving precisely that emptiness and lack of an heir. 'Being driven out of the land of Moab' is almost plausible geographically but is wrong, since Naomi voluntarily left Moab to return to Bethlehem (wrong_detail). 'Fearing Boaz would abandon Ruth' is almost plausible regarding the characters but is not the concern expressed, since Boaz had faithfully married her (common_misconception). 'The land debt owed to the elders' confuses this with the property-redemption transaction in 4:1-12, which is outside the scope of this blessing (wrong_scope).

content: The genealogy closing the book of Ruth (4:18-22) begins with whom as the first ancestor of the lineage?
options: Perez
Hezron
Salmon
Boaz
explanation: Ruth 4:18 reads: 'Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron.' Perez is the ancestor who opens the list. Hezron (wrong_detail) is the second person, the son of Perez, not the beginning. Salmon (wrong_detail) stands near the end of the list, the father of Boaz. Boaz (wrong_detail) is near the end, close to Obed.

content: According to the genealogy at the end of the book of Ruth, whom did Perez father to continue the lineage?
options: Ram
Hezron
Amminadab
Nahshon
explanation: Ruth 4:18 reads: 'Perez fathered Hezron.' Hezron is the son of Perez. Ram (wrong_detail) is the son of Hezron, a generation later. Amminadab (wrong_detail) is the son of Ram, two generations removed. Nahshon (wrong_detail) is the son of Amminadab, three generations removed.

content: In the genealogy closing the book of Ruth, who is recorded as the father of Boaz?
options: Salmon
Nahshon
Obed
Hezron
explanation: Ruth 4:21 reads: 'Salmon fathered Boaz.' Salmon is the father of Boaz. Nahshon (wrong_detail) is the grandfather of Boaz, the generation before Salmon. Obed (wrong_detail) is the son of Boaz, a later generation, not his father. Hezron (wrong_scope) belongs to the early generations of the list, far removed from Boaz.

content: According to the concluding verse of the genealogy, whom did Obed father before the lineage reaches David?
options: Jesse
Salmon
Samuel
Saul
explanation: Ruth 4:22 reads: 'Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.' Jesse is the son of Obed and the father of David. Salmon (wrong_detail) belongs to an earlier generation, the grandfather of Obed. Samuel (wrong_scope) is the prophet who anointed David but does not appear in this genealogy. Saul (wrong_scope) is the first king and does not belong to the lineage of Perez listed here.

content: If Perez is counted as the first generation, in what position does Boaz stand in the ten-name genealogy at the end of the book of Ruth?
options: The seventh generation
The sixth generation
The eighth generation
The fifth generation
explanation: Ruth 4:18-21 lists: Perez (1), Hezron (2), Ram (3), Amminadab (4), Nahshon (5), Salmon (6), Boaz (7). Thus Boaz is the seventh generation. 'The sixth generation' (wrong_detail) is the position of Salmon, the father of Boaz, off by exactly one step. 'The eighth generation' (wrong_detail) is the position of Obed, the son of Boaz, off by one step in the other direction. 'The fifth generation' (wrong_detail) is the position of Nahshon, off by two steps — a miscounting caused by skipping a name.

content: The genealogy at the end of the book of Ruth lists how many names in total, counting from Perez to David?
options: Ten names
Nine names
Eleven names
Seven names
explanation: Ruth 4:18-22 lists: Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David — ten names in total. 'Nine names' (wrong_detail) results from forgetting to count David in the final verse. 'Eleven names' (wrong_detail) comes from counting one extra person, off by one generation. 'Seven names' (wrong_detail) only counts up to Boaz and omits the last three generations: Obed, Jesse, and David.

content: Why does the genealogy that closes the book of Ruth stop precisely at the name David and not extend to later generations?
options: To highlight the lineage leading to King David
Because David was Jesse's only surviving youngest son
Because David personally wrote the book of Ruth
Because after David the genealogy shifts to the line of Saul
explanation: Ruth 4:17,22 directs the entire genealogy toward its climax in David: 'Obed... was the father of Jesse, the father of David,' showing that the purpose is to exalt King David's royal lineage. 'David was Jesse's only surviving youngest son' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Jesse had many sons and David was only the youngest, not the only one. 'David personally wrote the book' (common_misconception) has no basis in the text. 'Shifts to the line of Saul' (wrong_scope) is incorrect because Saul does not belong to the genealogy of Perez and is not mentioned here.

content: In the genealogy at the end of the book of Ruth, which of the following pairs of names correctly represents an immediate father-son relationship?
options: Amminadab fathered Nahshon
Ram fathered Amminadab, and then Amminadab fathered Salmon
Nahshon fathered Boaz
Hezron fathered Amminadab
explanation: Ruth 4:19-20 states: 'Amminadab fathered Nahshon' — this is the correct immediate father-son pair. 'Amminadab fathered Salmon' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Salmon was the son of Nahshon. 'Nahshon fathered Boaz' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Salmon stands between Nahshon and Boaz. 'Hezron fathered Amminadab' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Hezron fathered Ram, and Amminadab was the son of Ram.

content: Compared with the genealogy that opens the Gospel of Matthew, what is a NOTABLE difference in the genealogy at the end of the book of Ruth?
options: The genealogy in Ruth does not mention any women's names within the chain of ten names
The genealogy in Ruth ends at Solomon rather than David
The genealogy in Ruth begins with Abraham instead of Perez
The genealogy in Ruth lists Boaz before Salmon
explanation: Ruth 4:18-22 lists only a chain of ten male names from Perez to David, inserting no women's names; whereas Matthew later includes Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth. This requires comparing the two texts. 'Ends at Solomon' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because 4:22 stops at David — almost right since Solomon was David's son but falls outside the scope. 'Begins with Abraham' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because 4:18 opens with Perez — almost right since Abraham heads Matthew's genealogy but not Ruth's. 'Lists Boaz before Salmon' (wrong_detail) incorrectly reverses the order because 4:21 states that Salmon fathered Boaz.

content: A student wishes to argue that the story of Boaz redeeming the inheritance connects to the promise concerning the royal line. Which detail in the genealogy of 4:18-22 best supports that argument?
options: Boaz stands precisely in the middle of the chain running straight from Perez to David
Boaz is listed as the first ancestor of the entire genealogy
Boaz fathered Jesse, who was later anointed as king
Boaz was the son of Nahshon, the leader of the tribe of Judah
explanation: Ruth 4:18-22 places Boaz (the seventh generation) within the chain: Perez... Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed... down to David, so Boaz's act of redemption is precisely the link connecting to the royal line — this requires analyzing Boaz's position in the chain. 'The first ancestor of the entire genealogy' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because the opening ancestor is Perez (4:18), not Boaz. 'Boaz fathered Jesse' (wrong_detail) is almost right but off by one generation: Boaz fathered Obed, and it was Obed who fathered Jesse (4:21-22). 'Son of Nahshon, leader of the tribe of Judah' (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Boaz's father was Salmon, not Nahshon, and the detail about the tribal leader does not appear in this passage.

content: According to the ancient Israelite custom mentioned in this passage, what did people exchange with one another to confirm a redemption or transfer of property?
options: A sandal
A ring
A silver talent
A staff
explanation: Ruth 4:7 records the ancient Israelite custom: to confirm a redemption or exchange, one man would remove his sandal and give it to the other. A ring is a confirming sign of authority elsewhere in Scripture but not here (wrong_detail). 'A silver talent' confuses this with a purchase price rather than an object of witness (wrong_detail). 'A staff' is unrelated to this redemption custom (wrong_scope).

content: When the close relative told Boaz to buy the right of redemption for himself, what gesture did he make to confirm it?
options: Removed his own sandal
Struck hands with Boaz
Signed his name on a tablet
Knelt before the elders
explanation: Ruth 4:8 records: the relative said 'Buy it for yourself,' then removed his sandal. 'Struck hands' is a gesture of agreement elsewhere in Scripture but not here (wrong_detail). 'Signed his name on a tablet' is a later practice that does not match the text (common_misconception). 'Knelt before the elders' is not described in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: Before the elders and all the people, Boaz declared that he had purchased all the property that had belonged to Elimelech and his two sons — from whose hand?
options: Naomi
Ruth
Boaz
Orpah
explanation: Ruth 4:9 records Boaz saying he had purchased all the property of Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon from the hand of Naomi. Ruth is the one being married, not the owner selling the property (wrong_detail). Boaz is the buyer; he cannot also be the seller (wrong_scope). Orpah had returned to Moab in chapter 1 and has no connection to this property (wrong_scope).

content: Boaz said that the reason he married Ruth was to preserve what for the deceased?
options: The name of the dead man on his inheritance
The tomb of the dead man in Bethlehem
The silver and gold of the dead man
The right of eldership at the city gate
explanation: Ruth 4:10 records that Boaz married Ruth 'to perpetuate the name of the dead on his inheritance, so that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place.' 'The tomb' is not the stated purpose (wrong_detail). 'Silver and gold' misunderstands the goal as preserving wealth rather than a name (common_misconception). 'The right of eldership' has no connection to marrying Ruth (wrong_scope).

content: When blessing Boaz, the people and the elders prayed that the LORD would make Ruth like which two women who built up the house of Israel?
options: Rachel and Leah
Sarah and Rebekah
Leah and Rebekah
Rachel and Sarah
explanation: Ruth 4:11 records the blessing: 'May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel.' 'Sarah and Rebekah' were earlier matriarchs but are not the two named here (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Leah and Rebekah' is half correct but pairs the wrong second name (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Rachel and Sarah' is also half correct but substitutes Sarah for Leah (almost-right, wrong_detail).

content: In the blessing, the people prayed that Boaz would prosper in Ephrathah and be famous in which location?
options: Bethlehem
Moab
Hebron
Jerusalem
explanation: Ruth 4:11 records the blessing: 'May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem.' Moab was Ruth's homeland and where the family had fled, not the place blessed with fame (near_passage). Hebron is another city in Judah and does not appear here (wrong_detail). Jerusalem had not yet become the capital at this time and is not mentioned in the verse (wrong_scope).

content: The people compared Boaz's house to the house of Perez. Perez was the son whom Tamar bore to whom?
options: Judah
Boaz
Elimelech
Solomon
explanation: Ruth 4:12 records the blessing that Boaz's house would be like 'the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah.' Boaz himself is the one being blessed and could not be the father of Perez (almost-right, wrong_detail). Elimelech was Naomi's deceased husband and is unrelated to Perez's lineage (wrong_scope). Solomon was a later king, born many generations after Perez (common_misconception).

content: The blessing mentions Perez and prays for the offspring the LORD would give Boaz through Ruth. What does the overall blessing chiefly emphasize for Boaz?
options: Abundant and renowned offspring
A bountiful harvest the following year
Peace with neighboring nations
Rebuilding the temple in Bethlehem
explanation: Ruth 4:11-12 prays that the woman entering his house would be like Rachel and Leah, and that Boaz's house would be like Perez's 'through the offspring that the LORD will give you' — the focus is on abundant, renowned offspring. 'A bountiful harvest' draws from the harvesting context but is not the content of the blessing (near_passage). 'Peace with neighboring nations' is not mentioned here (wrong_scope). 'Rebuilding the temple' belongs to a later era and is entirely out of context (wrong_scope).

content: Why did the author of Ruth pause to explain the custom of removing the sandal before narrating Boaz's acquisition of the right of redemption?
options: Because it was an ancient custom that later readers might no longer understand
Because Boaz had violated the law and needed justification
Because the elders would not accept a verbal covenant
Because Ruth was Moabite and required a special procedure
explanation: Ruth 4:7 opens with 'Now this was the custom in former times in Israel...' — the editorial note shows that the sandal custom was old and later readers might not understand it, so the author explains it for verse 8 (the removal of the sandal) to be understood. 'Boaz violated the law' is wrong since he was exercising a legitimate right of redemption (common_misconception). 'The elders would not accept a verbal covenant' contradicts verses 9-11, where they serve as witnesses and pronounce a blessing (wrong_detail). 'Because Ruth was Moabite' is an inference beyond the text — the sandal custom applied to redemption in general, not because of Ruth's ethnic origins (wrong_scope).

content: Compared to the close relative who quietly removed his sandal and withdrew, what does Boaz's public action at the city gate reveal about how he fulfilled the right of redemption differently?
options: He declared it before witnesses to preserve the name of the deceased
He paid a higher price to eliminate the other relative
He asked the elders to exempt him from the obligation to marry
He kept the transaction private to avoid future disputes
explanation: Ruth 4:9-10 records Boaz publicly calling everyone as witnesses that he was buying the property AND taking Ruth as his wife 'to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance' — in stark contrast to the relative who merely withdrew (4:8). 'Paying a higher price to eliminate the other' is wrong because the relative voluntarily declined out of fear of jeopardizing his own inheritance (common_misconception). 'Asking to be exempted from the marriage obligation' is the opposite: Boaz himself voluntarily took Ruth as his wife (wrong_detail). 'Keeping the transaction private' contradicts his deliberate calling of public witnesses (wrong_detail).
